title: Quantization: hotspot migration & kernel fallback investigation
content:
TL;DR:
We observed intermittent P95/P99 latency spikes on INT8/AWQ model variants that correlate with a kernel-path switch when sequence length distribution skews mid-request (non-uniform batches). Spikes occur when (a) KV-cache hits are partial across batches and (b) the runtime switches from an optimized packed-GEMM path to a generic slower kernel. FP8 variants are less affected but still show throughput variance due to thread migration and memory packing churn.

Background / problem statement:
- Context: running perf regressions on 13B-class open model family (customer workload trace). Goal: understand why INT8/AWQ variants exhibit rare but high-latency tails under realistic non-uniform batch mixes (hot short prompts + occasional long-context requests).
- Symptoms observed in prod-like sim: 99th percentile latency jumps 2–3x for ~1–2s windows while throughput drops by 30–60%. CPU-side traces show increased kernel dispatch time and GPU kernel occupancy drops.

Quick observations (what we saw):
- Repro frequency: ~1/2000 requests under the traced workload in our local cluster, higher when the long-request ratio > 8%.
- Affected quant formats: INT8 (GPTQ/AWQ) worst, FP8 shows smaller variance but still non-negligible.
- Kernel behavior: switch from "packed GEMM kernel (fast)" -> "generic matmul fallback" on per-layer basis when per-batch effective sequence length distribution crosses internal thresholds (packing heuristics).
- Memory effects: repeated switches cause temporary buffer churn and fragmentation inside the allocator (observed via internal allocator metrics), leading to increased memcpy and kernel launch serialization.

Repro recipe (minimal):
1) Use rdw-profiling harness on dev-gpu-8 (A100-80GB) with model: llama-13b-ish open checkpoint converted to AWQ-int8 and a separate FP8 build.
2) Client simulation: 2500 requests over 10m with mix: 92% short prompts (len 32), 8% long prompts (len 2048). Inter-arrival poisson lambda tuned to replicate burstiness.
3) Runtime flags: batching enabled (adaptive), kernel-packing heuristics at default.
4) Collect: nsys timeline, rdw-trace (per-kernel timestamps), allocator histograms (rdw-alloc --hist), and perf counters (L2, dram bw).

Representative commands:
- run client: python tools/sim_client.py --trace-file tests/real_traces/mix_s92_l8.json --duration 600 --concurrency 64
- start profile: rdw-profiling start --out /tmp/run-0420.nsys; rdw-collect-trace --alloc --kernels

Raw (median) numbers from local run (example window showing spike):
- AWQ-INT8: tokens/s (sustained) 12.3k -> during spike 4.9k; P50 28ms, P95 110ms -> P95 during spike 260ms; GPU util drop 82% -> 47%
- GPTQ-INT8: tokens/s 11.6k -> 5.1k; P95 95ms -> 230ms
- FP8-opt: tokens/s 13.8k -> 9.8k; P95 70ms -> 140ms
- Memory churn: allocator fell into 3x memcpy events per request in spike windows vs baseline 0.8x

Signals from traces:
- Nsight/rdw-trace shows on some long-requests the runtime recomputes packing plan at layer 9–12 because KV cache hit mask differs across batch elements (some elements have cached past tokens, others not). Packing plan recompute triggers fallback to generic kernel for subsequent layers until packing buffer is rebuilt.
- Kernel durations: fast packed-kernel median 0.8–1.2ms per layer, generic matmul 3.6–5.4ms per layer (so 3–4x slower) which explains tail.
- Thread migration: host-side traces show worker threads moving between NUMA domains when a packing allocation exceeds local pool; that correlates with small but measurable CPU stall before re-launching kernels.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Packing heuristic threshold too brittle: small differences in per-example KV masks cause complete pack invalidation rather than incremental handle.
2) Allocator fragmentation: repeated packing rebuilds cause allocator to hand out non-contiguous buffers forcing extra memcpy and increased kernel launch serialization.
3) Kernel selection policy: policy prefers correctness-safe generic kernels when packing is partially valid; it may be overly conservative for AWQ quant decoders.
4) FP8 codepath pays a lower penalty because kernel implementations keep contiguous scratch space even on partial pack invalidation.

Potential mitigations to test (fast wins first):
- Tweak packing heuristics to allow partial pack reuse: allow per-layer partial-rows reuse instead of full-plan invalidation. Flag: --pack-tolerance=0.15 (experiment).
- Increase pre-allocated packing pool to reduce allocator churn: runtime config pack_pool=1.5x for 13B runs.
- Add a transient "degraded packing" kernel that accepts partially packed inputs but applies a tiny memcpy prologue in-GPU to align rows (cheaper than full generic kernel).
- Conservative: disable pack invalidation for the first N layers of long-request (cheap fast path) to see if tail frequency decreases.

Planned experiments (next 7 days):
A) Sensitivity sweep on pack-tolerance: [0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20] with same client trace. Measure spike frequency and average P95.
B) Allocator stress: run worst-case churn (randomized long/short bursts) with pack_pool sizes [1.0, 1.25, 1.5, 2.0]. Log memcpy counts.
C) Kernel-probe: implement a cheap GPU memcpy prologue inside packing kernel and compare latency (A/B).
D) FP8 vs INT8 isolation: run identical workload on FP8 and AWQ build but freeze packing plans (force reuse) to measure intrinsic quant overhead vs packing mechanics.

Preliminary results from quick A run (pack-tolerance=0.10):
- Spike frequency dropped from 1/2000 -> 1/8200 requests (good).
- Tokens/s median unchanged; P95 tail improved by ~40% during windows.
- Small regressions observed in single-request quality for certain AWQ-mapped heads (need QA checks).

Risks / caveats:
- Allowing partial pack reuse could introduce subtle numerical degradation for some AWQ layouts — need automated evals on our validation set (QA dev set + perplexity on wikitext subset).
- Increasing pool sizes increases memory footprint which may reduce effective concurrency on Dedicated boxes. Need cost-vs-latency tradeoffs.
- Changes to kernel prologues add maintenance burden across GPU architectures (ampere vs hopper differences).

Immediate action items (owners):
- Aisha: land pack-tolerance flag + simple partial-reuse prototype; run sweep A by EOD + collect traces. (ETA 3d)
- Luca: add allocator histogram sampling into production dev harness; create perf dashboard for memcpy events. (ETA 5d)
- Priya: run quality regression on AWQ-int8 for partial pack reuse; report any >0.5% delta in QA EM / perplexity regressions. (ETA 4d)
- Ben: prototype small memcpy-prologue kernel variant and microbench it on 1 GPU. (ETA 7d)

Notes / brainstorm (loose ideas):
- Could we implement pack-plan versioning that decays instead of invalidating? e.g., keep last N plans and diff incoming masks for cheap reuse.
- Consider a runtime hint API from client: if client can signal that occasional long requests are expected, runtime can preserve larger packing state. Useful for known workspace workloads.
- For Dedicated customers, expose packing_pool config in Console with estimated memory impact and latency benefits so SRE/infra can tune per-tenant.

Appendix: traces / mini logs (snippets)
- rdw-trace (layer 10) excerpt: "t=234.120 kernel=packed_gemm dur=1.02ms
 t=234.124 kernel=recompute_pack_plan dur=6.4ms
 t=234.131 kernel=generic_matmul dur=4.9ms
"
- allocator log snippet: "alloc(size=3.9MB) -> pool0 free 2.0MB, fallback to pool1, memcpy 3.9MB"

If you want to reproduce I can drop the sim trace + nsys tarball (about 1.2GB) into the linked artifacts. Let's iterate on pack-tolerance first — that gave the largest immediate win in the mini-sweep.
